# ECDF

## What: a step function of the sorted data

For a sample $\hat{X}_1, \ldots, \hat{X}_n$, the ECDF is the share of observations at or below $x$:
$$\hat{F}(x) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}(\hat{X}_{i} \leq x).$$

* Packages the sorted data as a function for visualization and resampling
* Jumps of $1/n$ at each observation

## Example: monthly earnings of 935 US workers, 1980.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
X <- wooldridge::wage2[, 'wage']   # monthly earnings of US workers, 1980 dollars
F_hat <- ecdf(X)
plot(F_hat, main=NA, pch=16, col=grey(0, .5),
  xlab='Monthly earnings (1980 dollars)',
  ylab='Proportion of workers at or below x')
rug(X)
```

## Why (1/2): Complementary empirics

Complements the histogram for data viz.

* Histograms better for shape: skewness, number and location of modes
* ECDFs better for precision: easily get quantiles, always the same for each student
* $\hat{F}$ is well suited for both discrete and continuous data

## How: monthly earnings of 935 workers {.smaller}

```{r}
#| output: false
n <- length(X)
mean(X <= 1000)                 # share of workers at or below 1000, by hand
F_hat(1000)                     # 1000 is the 0.62 quantile
quantile(X, probs=.62, type=1)  # inverting the ECDF gives 1000 back
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
plot(F_hat, main=NA, pch=16, col=grey(0, .5),
    xlab='Monthly earnings (1980 dollars)',
    ylab='Proportion of workers at or below x')
rug(X)
segments(-500, 0.62, 1000, 0.62, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8))
segments(1000, 0, 1000, 0.62, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8))
```

$1000$ dollars is the $0.62$ quantile

* $\hat{F}(1000) \approx 0.62~~$,&nbsp;&nbsp; share of workers earning $1000$ dollars or less is about $0.62$.
* $\hat{F}^{-1}(0.62) = 1000~~$,&nbsp;&nbsp; about $62\%$ of observations have a value of $1000$ or less.

## Why (2/2): Easier theory

ECDFs make theory easier

* Students can see both $\hat{f}$, $\hat{F}$ before $f, F$
* No histogram/KDE bandwidth issues as $n \to \infty$.
* Inference via bootstrap for any statistic students use.

## Histogram Density and ECDF

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.2
breaks <- seq(0, 3200, by=100)   # bin width 2h=100
f_hat <- hist(X, breaks=breaks, plot=FALSE)
x0 <- 750                    # value to compare across both views
below <- f_hat[['mids']] < x0
col_x <- rgb(0, 0, 1, .5)
par(mfrow=c(1, 2), mar=c(4, 4.5, 2, 1))

hist(X, breaks=breaks, freq=FALSE, border=NA,
    col=ifelse(below, col_x, grey(.8)),
    main=NA, xlab='Monthly earnings', ylab='')
title(ylab=expression(hat(f)), line=3)

plot(F_hat, xlim=range(breaks), pch=16, col=grey(0, .5),
    main=NA, xlab='Monthly earnings', ylab='')
title(ylab=expression(hat(F)), line=3)
segments(x0, F_hat(x0), -2, F_hat(x0), col=col_x)
segments(x0, F_hat(x0), x0, -1, col=col_x)
points(x0, F_hat(x0), pch=16, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), cex=1.5)
```

# The Fundamental Theorem of Statistics

## What: the ECDF converges to the CDF

Population CDF: $F(x) = \text{Prob}(X \leq x)$.


As $n$ grows, the largest gap between $\hat{F}$ and $F$ shrinks to zero:
$$\sup_x \left| \hat{F}(x) - F(x) \right| \rightarrow 0.$$


## Example: Log-normal household incomes

```{r}
#| output: false
income_meanlog <- log(50000)
income_sdlog <- 0.6
F_pop <- function(x) plnorm(x, meanlog=income_meanlog, sdlog=income_sdlog) # CDF
r_pop <- function(n) rlnorm(n, meanlog=income_meanlog, sdlog=income_sdlog) # draws
pop_median <- qlnorm(.5, meanlog=income_meanlog, sdlog=income_sdlog)
pop_median
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.4
x_grid <- seq(0, 200000, length.out=500)
par(mfrow=c(1, 3))
for (n_sim in c(10, 100, 1000)) {
    X_sim <- r_pop(n_sim)
    plot(ecdf(X_sim), main=NA, pch=16, col=grey(0, .5), xlim=c(0, 200000),
        xlab='Income', ylab='Proportion at or below x')
    lines(x_grid, F_pop(x_grid), col=rgb(0, 1, 0, .8), lwd=1)
    title(paste0('n = ', n_sim), font.main=1)
}
```

## What the theorem says
The estimator $F_{n}$ is a random function.
$$\sup_x \left| F_{n}(x) - F(x) \right| \rightarrow 0.$$
The spread around $F$ (green) shrinks as $n$ grows.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.4
# Draw many independent samples for each n and overlay their ECDFs.
n_rep <- 50
par(mfrow=c(1, 3))
for (n_sim in c(10, 100, 1000)) {
    plot(NULL, xlim=c(0, 200000), ylim=c(0, 1), main=NA,
        xlab='Income', ylab='Proportion at or below x')
    for (r in seq(n_rep)) {
        X_rep <- r_pop(n_sim)
        plot(ecdf(X_rep), add=TRUE, col=grey(0, .15),
            verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, col.01line=NA)
    }
    lines(x_grid, F_pop(x_grid), col=rgb(0, 1, 0, .8), lwd=2)
    title(paste0('n = ', n_sim), font.main=1)
}
```

## Why: the sample can stand in

* $\hat{F}(1000)$ is a fact, and also an estimate of $F(1000)$.
* Resampling from $\hat{F}$ is nearly the same as sampling from $F$

# Bootstrap

## What: resampling from the ECDF

* Draw $n$ observations from the data, with replacement. 
 Each observation is a draw from $\hat{F} \approx F$.
* Compute the statistic on the bootstrap sample.
* Repeat $B$ times.

This gives the *bootstrap distribution*, which is an estimate of the sampling distribution.

## Why (1/2): internalize sampling variability

Every step is visible and the distribution is more concrete.

```{r}
#| output: false
X <- wooldridge::wage2[, 'wage']
n <- length(X)
X_median <- median(X)
X_median
# Breaks with a common bin width, so the bootstrap histograms on both Why slides are comparable.
boot_breaks <- function(x, width=5) {
    seq(floor(min(x) / width) * width, ceiling(max(x) / width) * width, by=width)
}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.2
local({
    divideX <- c(.6, .65)
    divideY <- c(0, .32, .33, .65, .70, 1)
    useFraction <- .9
    Fraction2 <- 0:1 + c(1, -1) * (1 - useFraction) / 2
    rescaleY <- function(x) (x - .33) / .67
    divideY3 <- (c(NA, NA, .33, .65, .70, 1) - .33) / .67
    leftPad <- .05

    set.seed(2)
    boot_list <- lapply(1:3, function(b) sample(X, replace=TRUE))

    PlotSample <- function(data, star=FALSE, lineM=NULL, ylabels=TRUE) {
        plot(ecdf(data), xlim=c(0, 3100), ylim=c(0, 1), axes=FALSE,
            xlab='', ylab='', main=NA, do.points=FALSE, verticals=TRUE,
            col='gray30', lwd=2, xaxs='i', yaxs='i')
        axis(side=1, at=c(0, 2000))
        axis(side=2, labels=ylabels)
        if (length(lineM)) {
            segments(x0=c(0, lineM), y0=c(.5, .5), x1=c(lineM, lineM), y1=c(.5, 0),
                col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lty=2)
            axis(side=1, at=lineM, if (star) expression(tilde(m)^r) else expression(tilde(m)),
                col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), col.axis=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8))
        }
        invisible(NULL)
    }

    ### Sample: the one dataset we actually have
    par(fig=c(divideX[1] * (1/3 + 1/3 * Fraction2), divideY3[5:6]),
        mar=.1 + c(2, 0, 0, 0), mex=.8)
    PlotSample(X, lineM=X_median)

    ### Resamples, drawn from the sample with replacement
    ### Only the leftmost panel carries y-axis labels; the row shares one scale
    par(fig=c(divideX[1] * (0/3 + 1/3 * Fraction2) + c(leftPad, 0), divideY3[3:4]), new=TRUE)
    PlotSample(boot_list[[1]], star=TRUE, lineM=median(boot_list[[1]]), ylabels=TRUE)
    par(fig=c(divideX[1] * (1/3 + 1/3 * Fraction2), divideY3[3:4]), new=TRUE)
    PlotSample(boot_list[[2]], star=TRUE, lineM=median(boot_list[[2]]), ylabels=FALSE)
    par(fig=c(divideX[1] * (2/3 + 1/3 * Fraction2), divideY3[3:4]), new=TRUE)
    PlotSample(boot_list[[3]], star=TRUE, lineM=median(boot_list[[3]]), ylabels=FALSE)

    ### Resampling distribution of the median, centered at m-tilde, not at an unknown truth
    par(fig=c(divideX[2], 1, 0, .5), new=TRUE)
    par(mar=c(4.1, 0, 0, 1))
    set.seed(2)
    boot_meds <- sapply(1:999, function(b) median(sample(X, replace=TRUE)))
    hist(boot_meds, xlim=range(boot_meds), breaks=boot_breaks(boot_meds), border=NA,
        axes=FALSE, col=rgb(.8, 0, 0, .5), freq=FALSE, main=NA, yaxs='i', xlab='', ylab='')
    abline(v=X_median, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lty=2)
    axis(1, round(range(boot_meds), 1))
    axis(1, at=X_median, expression(tilde(m)), col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), col.axis=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8))

    ### Arrows
    par(mar=c(2.1, 0, 0, 0))
    par(fig=c(0, 1, 0, 1), usr=c(0, 1, 0, 1))
    arrows(lwd=1.5, length=.125,
        x0=divideX[1] * (.29 + .42 * ppoints(5)[c(1, 3, 5)]),
        x1=divideX[1] * seq(.3, .7, length=3),
        y0=rescaleY(divideY[4:5] %*% c(.2, .77)) - .05,
        y1=rescaleY(divideY[4] - c(.6, 1, .6) * (divideY[5] - divideY[4])) - .05)
    arrows(divideX[1], c(.1, .2, .3), length=.125, divideX[2], lwd=1.5)

    ### Text
    text(.4, .8, adj=0, 'Sample')
    text((divideX[2] + 1) / 2, .55, adj=.5, 'Resampling Distribution')
    text(0.01, divideY3[4] + .03, adj=0, 'Resamples (r)')
})
```


## Why (2/2): Inference without formulas or distributional assumptions {.smaller}

```{r}
#| output: false
B <- 9999
boot_medians <- rep(NA, B)
for (b in seq_along(boot_medians)) {
    X_b <- sample(X, replace=TRUE)   # some workers repeated, some left out
    boot_medians[b] <- median(X_b)
}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
par(mfrow=c(1, 2))

hist(boot_medians, breaks=boot_breaks(boot_medians), border=NA, freq=FALSE, main=NA,
    col=rgb(.8, 0, 0, .5),
    xlab='Bootstrap Median')
#abline(v=X_median, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lwd=2)
abline(v=quantile(boot_medians, probs=c(0.025, 0.975)), col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lwd=2)
xticks <- axTicks(1)

### Same 95% interval, read off the ECDF of the resampling distribution
ci <- quantile(boot_medians, probs=c(0.025, 0.975))
xr <- range(boot_medians)
plot(ecdf(boot_medians), do.points=FALSE, verticals=TRUE, col=rgb(.8, 0, 0, 1), lwd=2,
    xlim=xr, ylim=c(0, 1), xaxs='i', yaxs='i', xaxt='n',
    main=NA, xlab='Bootstrap Median', ylab=expression(hat(F)))
axis(1, at=xticks)
segments(x0=c(xr[1], ci[1], xr[1], ci[2]), y0=c(.025, .025, .975, .975),
    x1=c(ci[1], ci[1], ci[2], ci[2]), y1=c(.025, 0, .975, 0),
    col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lwd=2)
```

* Middle $95\%$ = the *percentile* confidence interval
* P-values: shift histogram to impose the null, see where the actual statistic falls
* Swap `median` for almost any other statistic: `mean`, `var`, `IQR`


# How to teach this?

## Ways to incorporate

1 Day Theory + 1 Day Lab.

If using a standard business textbook (e.g., Camm et al.),

Replace one week's worth of $t$-distributions and $z$-tables with these slides+lab

* *"complex formulas and distribution tables should be de-emphasized or eliminated."* ([GAISE](https://asacollegegaise.org/recommendations))


## Students will gain a modern foundation ([GAISE](https://asacollegegaise.org/recommendations))

Better descriptions as good practice

* *"Real data"* 
* *"Identify and interpret appropriate graphs"* 
* Create graphs *"beyond just simple boxplots"*

Intuitive and general understanding of inference

* *"Concepts over formulas"*
* *"Software to explore concepts"*
* *"Active learning"*

## Can eventually teach modern statistics deeply

* ECDFs early + histogram density
* CLT (less emphasis) $\to$ LLN $\to$ FTS $\to$ Bootstrap
* Bootstrap CI for means, medians, proportions, ...
* Simulations show how things work theoretically 
* Agentic coding for reproducible reports

You can cut many weeks of material that many students either hate or struggle with or never use.

## Even the 1-Day lab helps enormously 
*"professional software"* recommended by the [ASA (2014)](https://www.amstat.org/docs/default-source/amstat-documents/guidelines2014-11-15.pdf)

  * Excel: *"**we do not recommend it**"*, *"not ideal as a **programming** or **reproducible analysis** environment."*
  * RStudio: already modern, real data via `library(Ecdat)`
  * Claude/ChatGPT Desktop: new possibility (fully agentic) 

A conservative step forward: RStudio + Claude Browser

  * Students write and run an `R` script.
  * Upload to Claude for review
    * *What is going on?*
    * *Add comments.*


## Integrating AI {.smaller}
The conservative step is not clearly the best, but it's progress. 

No guarantee AI is always right. 
No guarantee the instructor is always right. (Who here has made no mistakes?)
In my experience, Claude/ChatGPT is excellent at statistics, especially Stats I.

Today, I think *costs to students* are not even close:

* a rare bad comment/explanation $<$ not exploiting agentic coding
* many ways to add AI safeguards 

A future progressive could have students work with `R` scripts only using AI (not RStudio) 


# Building on this downstream (Stats II)

```{r}
#| include: false
# Monthly earnings, split by whether the worker lives in an SMSA.
x_hat <- wooldridge::wage2[, 'wage']
urban <- wooldridge::wage2[, 'urban']
x_rural <- x_hat[urban == 0]
x_urban <- x_hat[urban == 1]
# Welch t-test of the urban minus rural mean.
t_res <- t.test(x_urban, x_rural)
# Group medians, and the urban ECDF to evaluate at the rural median.
med_rural <- median(x_rural)
med_urban <- median(x_urban)
F_urban <- ecdf(x_urban)
```

## Example: Are wages higher in the city?

One student: *yes, obviously*.

Another: *obviously not; my uncle owns a farm and he's rich*.

Let's look at real data

* Monthly earnings of $935$ US workers in 1980, rural vs urban (lives in an SMSA).
* a $t$-test finds urban workers earn $`r round(t_res$estimate[1] - t_res$estimate[2])`$ dollars more per month on average ($95\%$ CI $[`r round(t_res$conf.int[1])`, `r round(t_res$conf.int[2])`]$).


## Alternative (1/2) {.smaller}

* Medians: urban $`r med_urban`$ vs rural $`r med_rural`$, a $`r med_urban - med_rural`$ dollar gap.
* Overlap: $\hat{F}_{urban}(`r med_rural`) \approx `r round(F_urban(med_rural), 2)`$, so $`r round(100 * F_urban(med_rural))`\%$ of urban workers earn at most the rural median.
* Think distributionally, don't automatically test

```{r}
two_cols <- c(rgb(.8, 0, 0, .5), rgb(0, 0, .8, .5))
n_2 <- c(length(x_rural), length(x_urban))
# Line width proportional to sqrt(n), the same scaling varwidth uses for the boxes.
lwd_2 <- 3 * sqrt(n_2 / max(n_2))
two_par <- par(mar=c(4.5, 4.2, 1, 1))

### One ECDF per group on the same axes, line width scaled to group size
plot(ecdf(x_rural), col=two_cols[1], lwd=lwd_2[1], main=NA,
    verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, col.01line=NA, xlim=range(x_hat),
    xlab='Monthly earnings (1980 dollars)', ylab='Proportion of workers')
plot(ecdf(x_urban), col=two_cols[2], lwd=lwd_2[2], add=TRUE,
    verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, col.01line=NA)
# Mark the urban ECDF at the rural median.
segments(med_rural, 0, med_rural, F_urban(med_rural), col=grey(0, .6), lty=2)
segments(-500, F_urban(med_rural), med_rural, F_urban(med_rural), col=grey(0, .6), lty=2)
legend('bottomright', legend=paste0(c('Rural', 'Urban'), ' (n=', n_2, ')'),
    col=two_cols, lty=1, lwd=lwd_2, bty='n', cex=.8)
par(two_par)
```

## Alternative (2/2) {.smaller}

* Wider boxes mean more workers in that group.
* Boxplot notches are bootstrap $95\%$ intervals for the median.
* CI can be in/out of IQR. No overlap $\Rightarrow$ medians differ.

```{r}
#| output: false
# Bootstrap the median within each group, keeping each group's size.
n_boot <- 999
boot_med_rural <- rep(NA, n_boot)
boot_med_urban <- rep(NA, n_boot)
for (b in seq(n_boot)) {
    boot_med_rural[b] <- median(sample(x_rural, replace=TRUE))
    boot_med_urban[b] <- median(sample(x_urban, replace=TRUE))
}
# 95% bootstrap percentile intervals: one column per group.
med_ci_2 <- cbind(
    Rural=quantile(boot_med_rural, probs=c(.025, .975)),
    Urban=quantile(boot_med_urban, probs=c(.025, .975)))
med_ci_2
```

```{r}
# Larger axis text, since the bullets above leave less room for the figure.
box_par <- par(mar=c(4.5, 4.8, 1, 1), cex.axis=1.4, cex.lab=1.4)

### Boxplots with the bootstrap intervals as notches, box width scaled to group size
bx_2 <- boxplot(list(Rural=x_rural, Urban=x_urban), plot=FALSE)
bx_2[['conf']] <- med_ci_2
bxp(bx_2, notch=TRUE, varwidth=TRUE, boxfill=two_cols,
    whisklty=0, staplelty=0, outpch=NA, main=NA,
    xlab='', ylab='Monthly earnings (1980 dollars)')
# Raw observations, in place of whiskers and outliers
stripchart(list(x_rural, x_urban), pch='-', col=grey(0, .2), cex=2, vert=TRUE, add=TRUE)
par(box_par)
```


## Many Groups Example: Education

* An alternative or complement to ANOVA

```{r}
#| output: false
x_hat <- wooldridge::wage2[, 'wage']
educ <- wooldridge::wage2[, 'educ']
# Group years of schooling: dropout, high school, some college, BA, graduate.
educ_g <- cut(educ, breaks=c(0, 11, 12, 15, 16, 18),
    labels=c('<12', '12', '13-15', '16', '17-18'))
n_g <- table(educ_g)
n_g

# Bootstrap the median within each education group, keeping each group's size.
n_boot <- 999
boot_med_g <- matrix(NA, n_boot, nlevels(educ_g))
colnames(boot_med_g) <- levels(educ_g)
for (b in seq(n_boot)) {
    for (g in levels(educ_g)) {
        x_b <- sample(x_hat[educ_g == g], replace=TRUE)
        boot_med_g[b, g] <- median(x_b)
    }
}
# 95% bootstrap percentile intervals: one column per education group.
med_ci <- apply(boot_med_g, 2, quantile, probs=c(.025, .975))
round(med_ci)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
educ_cols <- hcl.colors(nlevels(educ_g))
lwd_g <- 1.5 + 2.5 * (n_g - min(n_g)) / (max(n_g) - min(n_g))
educ_par <- par(mfrow=c(1, 2), mar=c(4.5, 4.2, 1, 1))

### One ECDF per education group on the same axes, line width scaled to group size
plot(NULL, xlim=range(x_hat), ylim=c(0, 1), main=NA,
    xlab='Monthly earnings (1980 dollars)', ylab='Proportion of workers')
for (g in seq_along(levels(educ_g))) {
    plot(ecdf(x_hat[educ_g == levels(educ_g)[g]]), add=TRUE,
        col=educ_cols[g], lwd=lwd_g[g],
        verticals=TRUE, do.points=FALSE, col.01line=NA)
}
legend('bottomright', legend=paste0(levels(educ_g), ' years (n=', n_g, ')'),
    col=educ_cols, lty=1, lwd=lwd_g, bty='n', cex=.8)

### Boxplots with the bootstrap intervals as notches, box width scaled to group size
bx <- boxplot(x_hat ~ educ_g, plot=FALSE)
bx[['conf']] <- med_ci
bxp(bx, notch=TRUE, varwidth=TRUE, boxfill=hcl.colors(nlevels(educ_g), alpha=.45),
    whisklty=0, staplelty=0, outpch=NA, main=NA,
    xlab='Years of education', ylab='Monthly earnings (1980 dollars)')
# Raw observations, in place of whiskers and outliers
stripchart(x_hat ~ educ_g, pch='-', col=grey(0, .2), cex=1, vert=TRUE, add=TRUE)
par(educ_par)
```

## Pre vs. Post Example: Canada-USA Incomes {.smaller}

Comparable income definitions for Canada and the USA, 2020.

* [Luxembourg Income Study, June 2026 release](https://www.lisdatacenter.org/data-access/lis-in-our-world-in-data-owid/), processed by [Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/explorers/incomes-across-distribution-lis).

```{r}
#| output: false
# LIS June 2026 release, processed by Our World in Data and downloaded 15 September 2026.
# Published thresholds describe people assigned household income divided by sqrt(household size).
# Both income concepts use annual 2021 international dollars, adjusted for inflation and PPP.
income <- read.csv('income_lis_2020.csv')
income_countries <- c('United States', 'Canada')
income_concepts <- c('market', 'disposable')
income_titles <- c('Market income', 'Disposable income')
income_lty <- c(1, 1)
income_cols <- c(rgb(0, 0, .8, .7), rgb(.8, 0, 0, .7))
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
income_par <- par(mfrow=c(1, 2), mar=c(4.5, 4.2, 2.2, 1))
for (j in seq_along(income_concepts)) {
    plot(NA, xlim=c(0, max(income$threshold_2021_ppp) / 1000), ylim=c(0, 1),
        main=income_titles[j], xlab='Annual income (thousands of 2021 PPP dollars)',
        ylab='Cumulative share of people')
    for (i in seq_along(income_countries)) {
        rows <- income[income$country == income_countries[i] &
            income$concept == income_concepts[j], ]
        rows <- rows[order(rows$percentile), ]
        lines(rows$threshold_2021_ppp / 1000, rows$percentile / 100,
            type='o', pch=16, cex=.6, col=income_cols[i], lwd=1, lty=income_lty[j])
    }
    legend('bottomright', legend=c('USA', 'Canada'), col=income_cols,
        lwd=2, lty=income_lty[j], cex=.85)
}
par(income_par)
```

Same figure for causal inference diagnostics (effect of min. wage on New Jersey vs. Pennsylvania)


## Whole Curriculum (Stats II) closer to [ASA](https://www.amstat.org/docs/default-source/amstat-documents/guidelines2014-11-15.pdf) {.smaller}

**Directly**

* *"A modern statistical theory course might, for example, include work on computer-intensive methods and non-parametric modeling"*
* *"Resampling methods (including bootstrapping and permutation tests)"*
* *"A smaller set of methods, rather than a comprehensive laundry list"*: one resampling loop that works for means, medians, correlations, regression slopes, ...

**Indirectly**

* *"Effective visual displays and compelling written summaries"*: `quarto` reports
* *"Nonparametric regression"*, *"smoothing/kernel estimation"*
* *"model assessment"*: bias-variance tradeoff, cross-validation, p-hacking
